*The algorithm:*

Step 0: Initialization Step. Guess ![ModifyingAbove u With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[0] ⇒ ![ModifyingAbove upper P With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[0] ∈ *M*. Then repeat:

Step 1: e‐step. e‐project ![ModifyingAbove upper P With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[*i*] to *D*, gives ![ModifyingAbove upper Q With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[*i*].

Step 2: m‐step. m‐project ![ModifyingAbove upper Q With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[*i*] to *M*, gives ![ModifyingAbove upper P With ampersand c period circ semicolon](images/c8-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>[*i*+1].

*Relation between EM and em:*

1.  M‐step and m‐step are the same
2.  E‐step and e‐step differ depending on the conditional expectation of *r*[*h*] given *r*[*v*]:

Note: Divergence need not be symmetric or satisfy the triangle inequality, but given “orthogonal” learning steps, a Divergence satisfies a generalized Pythagorean theorem, leading to a the same critical Chapman–Kolmogorov‐like propagation rule whether learning step assumes a Euclidean notion of distance (GD) or a KL divergence notion of distance (EG).

*Which Is Better?*

EM is more natural from statistical point of view, but the representation via a neural network does not correspond exactly to statistical inference, therefore em serves better as the approximator ideally suited to the neural network representation of the input–output relation. The two algorithms are asymptotically equivalent when *T* is large (in the framework of exponential families). If framework extended from exponential family to function space they are exactly equivalent. It may be that a hybrid of GD and EG, or of EM and em type learning, is best, and this will be explored further in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml) in an explicit loss bounds analysis on the learning process.

Amari’s Dually Flat formulation is a more natural structure for representing exponential families and neural nets than it might appear at first sight. In particular, the Kullback–Leibler measure is naturally represented in terms of the dual coordinates and their relations via Legendre transformation (with the introduction of appropriate potentials). The potentials, in turn, provide a natural formulation that is precisely that exhibited when using the “link formalism.” Similarly, the duality between the coordinates (via Legendre transformation) is precisely that exhibited in the neural net learning algorithms by [\[213\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0213) and [\[214\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0214) and described in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml).

While the e‐projection and m‐projection are natural geometric notions and certainly a strength of Amari’s program, they also represent a weakness. This weakness is perhaps most clearly illustrated in the learning algorithm version where the projection is determined and then the actual update is interpolated (between old data and estimator and new, projected data and estimator). In this instance we must fall back on the gradient descent algorithm, or some such arguments, in order to have stable updates. One approach might be to use the SA link algorithm since it results in a formalism that interpolates between GD and EG learning according to the weight magnitude. Further details on this approach are given in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml).

 

## 8.5 Exercises

 

1.  **8.1** Re‐derive the *α*‐connections for *α* = 1 and *α* = −1 and show that they are “dually flat.”
2.  **8.2** Introduce potentials on a dually flat space as described in [Section 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c8-sec-0006), then show how their Legendre transformation induces a natural difference measure that is a divergence. 
3.  **8.3** Prove the generalization of the Pythagorean theorem for dually flat spaces.
4.  **8.4** Show that em learning singles out the Kullback–Leibler Divergence as fundamental in dually flat space (this is akin to a Riemannian manifold giving rise to a fundamental locally flat spacetime reference and local Euclidean distance measure).

# 9  
Neural Net Learning and Loss Bounds Analysis

 

In this chapter, neural learning loss bounds derivations are given for the gradient descent learning process (GD) as well as other learning processing indicated in the link formalism. The link formalism provides a unified variational formalism for learning or “information dynamics” ([Section 9.2.1](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0010)). To start, however, a detailed, but brief, description of neural nets will be given starting with the single neuron ([Section 9.1.1](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0003)). [Section 9.1.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0007) describes neural nets and back‐propagation (which is then largely explored in the TensorFlow implementation described in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml)). [Section 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0013) describes the motivation for the link function *f*(*ω*) = sinh^( − 1)(*ω*). [Section 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0016) provides a loss bounds analysis for the link function *f*(*ω*) = sinh^(−1)(*ω*).

In Machine Learning we have identified good families of “update rules” that can perform neural net learning. In examination of update rules that are “good” it is possible in some cases to explicitly derive the error rate or loss during learning and quantify loss‐bounds on the overall learning process. In doing so there appears to be a learning phenomenology “regularization” for the better algorithms akin to the Newtonian Physics phenomenology of inertia in predicting motion. The Loss Bounds analysis reveals that statistical learning is feasible in these domains of application, i.e., they are effectively a proof of the feasibility of “statistical learning”. However, the description and results also indicate that the choice of learning “update rules” and optimization constraints can greatly impact the performance of the algorithms (to be further explored with SVMs in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml)). So the loss bounds method described is partly done to help understand what will likely be a good learning rule for developers optimizing a neural net or classifier for a particular input data environment.

 

## 9.1 Brief Introduction to Neural Nets (NNs)

In [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml) we saw brief mention of neural nets in an advanced mathematical setting where they are related to a manifold (a “neuromanifold”) that can be used to perform learning (with dimensionality given by the number of weights in the neural net in the case of a neuromanifold). In [Section 9.1.1](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0003) that follows, we start at the beginning of the computational neuron discussion, with a description of the Perceptron and Sigmoid neurons. In [Section 9.1.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0007), the classic description of back‐propagation is given, whereby a neural net can learn efficiently (akin to exponential to quadratic reduction in computational order in the Viterbi algorithm).

 

### 9.1.1 Single Neuron Discriminator

Shown in [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0001) is a single neuron discriminator with a simple activation function (a step function) also known as the perceptron.

 

#### 9.1.1.1 The Perceptron

The classic machine learning neural net classifier, the perceptron, will now be re‐derived. The notation of [\[109\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0109) will be followed so that use can then be made of Problem 1.3 from [\[109\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0109) where the proof of the perceptron learning is done. Let *X* = *R*^(*d*) be the input space. Let *Y* = {+1, − 1} be the output space (which denotes a yes/no decision typically). We will want to be able to adjust weight on the importance of different features in the input space in arriving at a decision, and then have a simple threshold rule to make that decision:

![Figure 9.1 Single Neuron with step (threshold) activation function. The inputs xk are multiplied by the weights ωk, and possibly have a bias applied, and the result is passed through a step function such that a(x, ω, b) = θ(ω⋅x − b), where θ(z) = 1if z > 0 and θ(z) = −1 if z ≤ 0.](images/c09f001.gif)

[**Figure 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0001) **Single Neuron with step (threshold) activation function.** The inputs *x*[*k*] are multiplied by the weights *ω*[*k*], and possibly have a bias applied, and the result is passed through a step function such that *a*(*x*, *ω*, *b*) = *θ*(*ω*⋅*x* − *b*), where *θ*(*z*) = 1if *z* > 0 and *θ*(*z*) = −1 if *z* ≤ 0.

Approve if

![equation](images/c9-disp-0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="italic"></mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <msubsup> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </msubsup> <mtext mathvariant="italic">&#969;ixi</mtext> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math> 

Deny if

![equation](images/c9-disp-0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="0.2em"/> <msubsup> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </msubsup> <mtext mathvariant="italic">&#969;ixi</mtext> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math> 

Let us treat the threshold value as a weight *ω*[0] = −*b* and associate it with an added *x* coordinate, *x*[0] = 1. Let’s also make use of the sign function: sign(*s*) = 1 if *s* > 0, and sign(*s*) = −1 if *s* < 0. The decision function *h*(*x*) is +1 if approved and −1 if denied:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo>sign</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

The classic perceptron learning algorithm then goes as follows ([Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0002)). Suppose at the current iteration, *t*, of the learning algorithm, we have weight vector *ω*(*t*). If we have not already arrived at a solution then some of the (*x*[1],*y*[1])…(*x*[*N*],*y*[*N*]) will be misclassified, i.e., *h*(*x*[*k*]) ≠ *y*[*k*] for various *k* values, and one of these misclassifications will be used in the **update rule**:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi> <mo mathvariant="bold-italic">+</mo> <mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi> </mfenced> <mo mathvariant="bold-italic">+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi> </mfenced> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi> </mfenced> </math> 

First note that: *y*(*t*)\[*ω*(*t*) ⋅ *x*(*t*)\] < 0 for each update (*y* has different sign than *ω* · *x*). Second, note: *y*(*t*)\[*ω*(*t* + 1) ⊕ *x*(*t*)\] > *y*(*t*)\[*ω*(*t*) ⋅ *x*(*t*)\] (so move toward positivity), where this last follows from *y*(*t*)\[*ω*(*t* + 1) ⋅ *x*(*t*)\] = *y*(*t*)\[*ω*(*t*) ⋅ *x*(*t*)\] + \[*y*(*t*)\]²\[*x*(*t*) ⋅ *x*(*t*)\]. This move toward positivity is shown in [Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0002).

Within the infinite space of all weight vectors, the perceptron algorithm finds a weight vector that works. This means that an infinite hypothesis space will be searched in a finite number of steps, so finite time, to find a solution. This search of an infinite hypothesis space in finite time will be one of the hallmarks of the Feasibility of Learning Proof (the “First Law of Machine Learning”).

![Figure 9.2 Perceptron update. The update rule shifts the position of the separating hyperplane such that classification errors eventually reduced to zero (assuming separable and that it does not get stuck in a local minimum of the minimization process).](images/c09f002.gif)

[**Figure 9.2**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0002) **Perceptron update.** The update rule shifts the position of the separating hyperplane such that classification errors eventually reduced to zero (assuming separable and that it does not get stuck in a local minimum of the minimization process).

To recap, the components of the Perceptron Learning Algorithm are:

1.  There is an input *x*.
2.  There is an unknown target function *f*: *X* → *Y*.
3.  There is a data set *D* of (input, output) examples (*x*[1],*y*[1]),…,(*x*[*N*],*y*[*N*]), where *y*[*n*] = *f*(*x*[*n*]).
4.  There is a learning algorithm that uses dataset *D* to pick a formula *g*: *X* → *Y* that approximates *f*.
5.  The algorithm chooses *g* from a set of candidate formulas under consideration, which we call the hypothesis set *H*. In the case of the perceptron, *h*(*x*) = sign(*ω*⋅*x*), *h* ∈ *H*.

The proof that the Perceptron Learning Algorithm converges to a solution follows the steps outlined in Problem 1.3 from [\[109\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0109) . Assuming the data is separable, there is a set of weights, *ω*\*[,] that separates the data:

1.  Have ![images](images/c9-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="italic">&#961;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>min</mo> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munder> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mi>&#8901;</mi> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> since separable means all classified correct, so signs of *y*[*n*] and *ω*^(\*) · *x*[*n*] always match, thus their product always positive.
2.  Have · *ω*(*t*)  *ω*^(\*) ≥ *ω*(*t* − 1)  · *ω*^(\*) + *ρ*, then with induction have *ω*(*t*) · *ω*^(\*) ≥*t* *ρ*.
3.  Have ‖*ω*(*t*)‖² ≤ ‖*ω*(*t* − 1)‖² + ‖*x*(*t* − 1)‖²,
4.  By induction have ‖*ω*(*t*)‖² ≤ *tR*², where ![images](images/c9-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>max</mo> <mi>n</mi> </munder> <mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mfenced> </math>.
5.  Can put together to now have: *t* ≤ *R*²‖*ω*^(\*)‖²/*ρ*².

Thus, an infinite space of weight vectors is searched in less than *R*²‖*ω*^(\*)‖²/*ρ*² steps (e.g., a finite number of steps).

 

#### 9.1.1.2 Sigmoid Neurons

Let us now consider connecting up a collection of neurons to make a neural net. If we try to work with the perceptrons, their step function activation is detrimental in that it fires all‐or‐nothing, leading to an unstable learning process when networked. Almost as a rule, we want our learning process, here parametrizing a neural net, to be such that a small input change leads to a small output change. This is automatically the case if the activation function and formalism overall is differentiable, then a chain rule relating change in input to change in output can be written (and small enough input will give small enough output). Thus, the shift to the sigmoid activation function neuron ([Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0003)) that is smooth and differentiable (“S shaped”) in the next section. This differentiability is then critical to establishing learning via backpropagation, where the chain rule is used, and where backward propagation through the network is done because it allows a recursion relation to be written with loss in one layer only dependent on loss in its output layer (akin to Viterbi recursion with one column only dependent on its prior column). This reduces the computational task to polynomial time from exponential time (as with the Viterbi algorithm in the HMM chapters), so it is a critical methodology for practical learning implementations.

![Figure 9.3 Single Neuron, Sigma activation function: the inputs xk are multiplied by the weights ωk, and possibly have a bias applied, and the result is passed through a function that is monotonically increasing, differentiable, with asymptotes (−1 or 0, and 1, typically): a(x, ω, b) = σ(ω⋅x − b).](images/c09f003.gif)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0003) **Single Neuron, Sigma activation function:** the inputs *x*[*k*] are multiplied by the weights *ω*[*k*], and possibly have a bias applied, and the result is passed through a function that is monotonically increasing, differentiable, with asymptotes (−1 or 0, and 1, typically): *a*(*x*, *ω*, *b*) = *σ*(*ω*⋅*x* − *b*).

 

#### 9.1.1.3 The Loss Function and Gradient Descent

Consider the simple activation function for the neuron: *a*(*x*) = *ω*⋅*x* (inner product between vector of weights and vector of instance feature components). The notation in this section will assume any bias value, from the standard notation *ω*⋅*x* − *b*, is absorbed into the “*ω*⋅*x*” notationally as an extra *ω*^(*n*+1) = −*b* component with associated *x*^(*n*+1) = 1 value. If the observed value is *y*(*x*), then our error, or loss, or cost associated with the neuron with its current learned *ω* values is:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> <mo> </mo> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> ![equation](images/c9-disp-0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo> </mo> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo> </mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#8711;</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mo>&#916;</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> </math> 

Let us choose a change in weights given by the negative gradient on the Loss function (Gradient Descent or GD), with magnitude modulated by *η*, a “learning rate”:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#916;</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8711;</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

This guarantees that the Loss will decrease with each learning step since:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo> </mo> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow> <mo>&#8711;</mo> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

From the gradient descent update rule we get:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

The description above can be thought of as describing information learning dynamics in terms of loss minimization subject to a learning rate, later ([Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0009)) we will see this can be fully encapsulated in a variational formulation in what follows. Most of this chapter explores the learning capabilities of a *single* neuron further, eventually crossing over to related SVM‐based learning in [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml). But first, let us briefly discuss how this will relate to multiple neuron systems in the form of neural nets, which will then be developed further in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml).

 

### 9.1.2 Neural Net with Back‐Propagation

Neural Nets with backpropagation learning are implemented in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml) using the Google TensorFlow package. In this section is shown the core theory of the backpropagation learning methodology up to Deep Learning (which is left to [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml)). In what follows we see that the core model/theory for neural networks is remarkably simple, yet their performance, if they work at all, is generally very good. What makes the difference all (good) or nothing? It’s a matter of having sufficient data to train the NN. If the neurons in the NN have a good activation function and a good learning rule, the amount of data needed is reduced. If there is sufficient data, however, any simple sigma activation and learning with gradient descent on the loss function (discussed next), will arrive at good results. Furthermore, the computation can be done efficiently (a must if success is premised on having immense amounts of data to process). We will see that the learning task can be distributed (multi and multicore CPUs) and vectorized (GPU), for multiple magnitude speedup in processing time.

 

#### 9.1.2.1 The Loss Function – General Activation in a General Neural Net

Consider the neural net shown in [Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0004).

Notes on the backpropagation derivation follow. The key idea is that we make use of the chain rule, but do so in a the form of a recursively defined expression to have an efficient computational implementation.

The activation function is now referenced by layer and neuron index in that layer (following the notational convention on weights indicated in [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0003)). In component notation this is:

![Figure 9.4 Neural Net, layered topology, fully connected between layers (“dense”). The weight label shown indicates the labeling scheme, with superscript denoting the layer, left subscript the neuron index coming from the layer indicated, to the neuron index shown in the right subscript in the next layer. Shown is the weight labeled for the fifth (lowest) input weight that connects into the third (lowest) neuron in the next layer.](images/c09f004.gif)

[**Figure 9.4**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0004) **Neural Net, layered topology, fully connected between layers (“dense”).** The weight label shown indicates the labeling scheme, with superscript denoting the layer, left subscript the neuron index coming from the layer indicated, to the neuron index shown in the right subscript in the next layer. Shown is the weight labeled for the fifth (lowest) input weight that connects into the third (lowest) neuron in the next layer.

![equation](images/c9-disp-0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">jk</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

If we work with neural nets with one node for final layer, then we can write the Loss in terms of the inputs and activation at that last neuron (layer “*L*,” related recursively to earlier layers of neurons):

![equation](images/c9-disp-0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#8594;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>x</mi> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> 

In the variational analysis that follows we can think of *L* a function of *ω* and *a* or of *z* = *ω*⋅*a*, where the latter variation works out simplest, so it will be used. The change in loss *δ* with change in “*z*” input can then be defined at the final layer and then related recursively to earlier layers:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Recall that ![images](images/c9-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> </math>, so ![images](images/c9-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> </math> if *k* = *j*, zero otherwise, so:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </math> 

which established the boundary term, we now need a recursive relation to complete the derivation:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Since ![images](images/c9-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">jk</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">jk</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> </math>:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">kj</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> </math> 

So,

![equation](images/c9-disp-0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>k</mi> </munder> <msubsup> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">kj</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msubsup> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Further elaboration on the above derivation, with more discussion of the critical role of sigmoid (differentiable) neurons can be found at [neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com](http://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com).

As with the single neuron, depending on how the learning on the weights is regularized for stability, we arrive at a learning, or update, rule on the weights. For the typical square weight regularizer, we get gradient descent. Variations on this will be examined in [Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-sec-0009). Critical to this learning process for neural nets is the existence of the above chain rule and a differentiable (stable) activation function. In [Chapter 11](#c11.xhtml), we will see that one of the simplest search heuristics is gradient descent, so this suggests that the neural net might be improved by use of one of the other, non‐differentiable, stochastic sampling heuristics described there. If this is used to efficiently approximate the gradient itself, used in gradient descent, we arrive at stochastic gradient descent neural net learning. But that is as far as it goes. To extend to the variety of other more stochastic search methodologies to be described in [Chapter 11](#c11.xhtml), the “differentiability” of that search outcome is a much less stable, and when compounded via the chain rule we see a very unstable learning process. This will not work in large multilayer neural nets trained used immense amounts of data – the instability will act as noise to weaken the overall net performance. This is why the neurons used in the neural net described in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml) tend to be sigmoid (differentiable) with simple regularization.

  

## 9.2 Variational Learning Formalism and Use in Loss Bounds Analysis

 

### 9.2.1 Variational Basis for Update Rule

In the online learning process, it is proposed that the weights remain unchanged unless forced to change by a “learning” process. (A “first law” of information dynamics analogous to Newton’s first law.) Instantaneous change, however, is not realizable physically and the same is assumed for information (whether or not a physical incarnation for the information is established). So when describing the response of the weights to a learning process it is also desirable to introduce an inertial property (“resistance” or “memory”). The resulting formalism achieves a balance between a tendency for the weights to remain unchanged referred to as the memory conservativeness, or inertia according to context and a change in the weights due to learning process (also referred to as correctness, or perhaps, the learning “force”). I'll refer to the latter principle as the second law of information dynamics due to its parallels with Newton's second law of dynamics, and, like its analogue, there is a variational formulation.

It is only in its variational formulation that an analysis of ‘information dynamics” really begins to go its own way – separate from the physical Newtonian analogue. In large part this is due to the easy entry of a new conceptual element into the formalism: Entropy. The definition of Entropy is best understood in a variational context, and it is often defined in such terms. Sometimes the variational aspect of entropy is implicit, such as in thermodynamics, where the fundamental equilibrium states are ones of maximum entropy. Sometimes, on the other hand, the variational aspect is made quite clear, such as in the Jaynesian school of thought, where the links to thermodynamics are forged by the Maximum Entropy Principle [\[112\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0112) .

When the second law of information dynamics is initially put into a variational formulation the measure of comparison between weight vectors is naturally defined by the Euclidean concept of “distance”:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math> 

which is the Gradient Descent (GD) algorithm.

Other distance metrics lead to updates other than that of the classical GD algorithm (where the loss function is taken to be the usual square loss in all of the functions considered here). Furthermore it soon becomes apparent that the introduction of information entropy (as explored by Shannon), allows for an altogether different measure of comparison – one that need not satisfy the usual metric properties implied by the usage of the term “distance.” The Kullback–Leibler measure indicated from [Chapter 8](#c08.xhtml) being an example of such, and one that leads to link function *f*(*ω*) = ln*ω*.

The existence of loss bounds for the updates expressible in terms of the “laws” of information dynamics might be taken as an indication of future successes of an information dynamics perspective.

 

### 9.2.2 Review and Generalization of GD Loss Bounds Analysis \[[213](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0213), [214](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0214)\]

The proof of the worst‐cast Loss Bounds centers on establishing the inequality

![equation](images/c9-disp-0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

For constraints a and b as general as possible, where *x*[*t*] is bounded by a 2‐norm or ∞‐norm, and the weights are bounded also, if necessary.

Begin with a review (and generalization) of the GD Loss Bounds analysis, where the variational basis for update rule is given as:

Properties of *d*(*ω*,*s*):

Or

![equation](images/c9-disp-0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> </math> 

where the latter choice η gives the broadcast range of possible *a*′s. Suppose we take *η* = *b*/(1 + 2*X*² *b*) always:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">min</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="italic">ab</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> ![equation](images/c9-disp-0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">min</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>when</mtext> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="italic">ab</mi> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>or</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math> 

Thus, we arrive at:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mtext>Condition for</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>GD</mi> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>lemma</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mn>5.1</mn> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mn>214</mn> </mfenced> </math> 

Thus, for GD with learning rate *η* above and ![images](images/c9-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> </math> we satisfy:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Once we know the constraints on *a* and *b* in the equation above, for the particular algorithm (GD in preceding), we can simply sum over a trial sequence to get the Worst Case Loss Bounds:

For GD Worst Case Loss Bounds, let ![images](images/c9-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> </math>:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> </mfenced> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Now sum on instances from *t* = 0 to *t* = *T* − 1, for GD:

![images](images/c9-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Loss</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>GD</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mtext>Loss</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>u</mi> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>T</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </math>,

Thus

![images](images/c9-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>Loss</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>GD</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mtext>Loss</mtext> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>u</mi> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </math>,

This result is equivalent to Lemma 5.2 in [\[213\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0213) .

Here we have polynomial groupings in *ω*⋅*x* and *u*⋅*x*, but not (*ω*⋅*x* − *u*⋅*x*), so the analysis cannot proceed as in the key GD step where this was possible (allowing for polynomial expression in *q*’s and *p*’s and no *ω* or *u* references. Because of this, EGU will need more involved bounds on *ω*⋅*x* ≤ *y*, as will be apparent when comparison is made in the following sinh^(−1)(*x*) link analysis.

 

## 9.3 The “sinh^(−1)(ω)” link algorithm (SA)

 

### 9.3.1 Motivation for “sinh^(−1)(ω)” link algorithm (SA)

Given a set of instances and outcomes, the initial goal in using Loss Bounds analysis to guide algorithm development was to consider an algorithm that settles (quickly) on predications from the “best expert,” where the experts will consist of the established neural net learning algorithms – Gradient Descent (GD) and un‐normalized Exponentiated Gradient Descent (EGU), where the implementation is done in the frame‐work of a neural net (NN) that learns via back‐propagation. To do this, initially, an algorithm was proposed that alternated between the GD update and the EGU update with latency in each update dependent on the successes of that algorithm. In other words, if the EGU update provided smaller losses than the last GD update – then the EGU update would again be used. In order to prevent pathological domination of one update over another, it was further proposed that the choice of next update have a stochastic element as well. The problem with this model was in the weight domains for GD vs EGU, GD having *R* for domain while EGU has *R*^+ or *R*^−. To remedy this an EGU‐like update was sought with domain *R*, which suggested that the update with link function sinh^(−1)(*w*) be used. The sinh^(−1)(*w*) algorithm (SA) is asymptotically like EGU on large *R*^+, and like negative EGU on large *R*^−, and crosses the origin as an odd function – i.e. it behaves like GD for weights near zero (near the origin). So in seeking an algorithm like EGU on *R*, the SA algorithm was obtained that also has regions of behavior akin to the GD algorithm. Since SA behaves like both GD and EGU depending on the magnitude of the weight it will be examined in an exact study of loss bounds for SA and this is the focus of what follows.

Link functions for GD, EGU^(+/−), and SA are shown in [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0005):

![Figure 9.5 Link functions for GD (linear), EGU+/− (left and right curves), and SA (sigmoid).](images/c09f005.gif)

[**Figure 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0005) Link functions for GD (linear), EGU^(+/−) (left and right curves), and SA (sigmoid).

Asymptotic properties of *f*(*ω*) = sinh^(−1)(*ω*): for |*ω*| ≫ 1: *f*(*ω*) ≅ ln(*ω*) + ln(2) for (*ω* > 0), so ~EGU^+, and *f*(*ω*) ≅ −ln(*ω*) − ln(2) for (*ω* < 0), so ~EGU^−, and for −1 ≪ *ω* ≪ 1: *f*(*ω*) ≅ *ω*, so ~GD.

Since sinh^(−1)(*ω*) = ln(*ω* + ![images](images/c9-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </math>) this suggests the parameterized generalization via *f*(*ω*) = ln(*ω* + ![images](images/c9-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> </mrow> </msqrt> </math>). General (positive) *γ* leads to a GD‐like update for small *ω*, but with a factor affecting the learning rate.

A statement of the learning algorithm for the sinh‐link algorithm (SA) is:

*   *Parameters:* 
    *   *L*: a loss function from *R* × *R* to \[0,∞)
    *   *S*: a start vector in *R*^(*N*) , and
    *   *η*: a learning rate in \[0,∞)
*    *Initialization:* Before first trial, set *ω*[1] = *S*
*   *Prediction:* upon receiving *t*th instance *x*[*t*], give prediction ![images](images/c9-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mspace width="0.2em"/> </math>\= *ω*[*t*] \* *X*[*t*]
*   *Update:* upon receiving the *t*th outcome *y*[*t*], update the weights according to the rule: ![equation](images/c9-disp-0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mfenced open="|" close=""><mtable> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> </math> 

 

### 9.3.2 Relation of sinh Link Algorithm to the Binary Exponentiated Gradient Algorithm

The SA link function is similar to the Binary Exponentiated Gradient algorithm (BEG) \[216\] link function ([Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0006)).

A transformation on the weights allows BEG to be reexpressed as SA. This is accomplished by simplifying the following:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>Z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">BEG</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi mathvariant="italic">BEG</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </math> 

where *L* < *ω*[*BEG*] < *M* ⟹ 0 < *Z* < ∞ ⇒ −∞ < *ω*[*s*] < ∞. Solving (call *ω*[*BEG*] = *y* for this):

## 9.4 The Loss Bounds Analysis for sinh^(−1)(*ω*)

The loss Bounds analysis for the *f*(*ω*) = sinh^(−1)(*ω*) link function is addressed next. The derivation follows the method of Kivinen and Warmuth and Jagota and Warmuth \[[213](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0213), [214](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0214)\] as summarized in Bylander [\[215\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0215) . The derivation in what follows was done in collaboration with Warmuth and Jagota.

The expression *d*(*u*, *ω*[*t* + 1]) − *d*(*u*, *ω*[*t*]) is now evaluated:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>u</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> </mfrac> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

Since the update rule is:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfenced open="|" close=""><mtable> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> 

And only the square loss case considered, we have

![equation](images/c9-disp-0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo> </mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>;</mo> <mspace width="2em"/> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mfenced open="|" close=""><mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>z</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

Thus, ![images](images/c9-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> and following [\[213\]](#b04.xhtml#b1-bib-0213) , the substitution ![images](images/c9-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo>exp</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>y</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> is made. Together with using the logarithmic form for the sinh^(−1) *s* this becomes:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>ln</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> </mfrac> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math> 

Now have:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo> </mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </math>

![equation](images/c9-disp-0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>cosh</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </math>

To get:

The loss Bound statement is now expressed in terms of function *F*, *F*(*ω*[*t*], *x*[*t*], *ω*[*t*]⋅*x*[*t*], *y*[*t*], *u*[*t*]⋅*x*[*t*], *η*) ≤ 0, where:

First consider max *F* for some choice of ![images](images/c9-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8901;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo> </mover> </math>:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>b</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo> </mover> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>b</mi> </math>

<mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>4</mn> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>R</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>where</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </math> 

So,

![equation](images/c9-disp-0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>and</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi>G</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>and</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>R</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>&#951;</mi> </mfrac> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mtext>or</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">Rb</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> </math> 

The tightest restriction in the second inequality is then found by obtaining the upper bound on *R*:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>sinh</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>cosh</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>ln</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

In order to establish the inequality:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>u</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8901;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mtext>where</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">Rb</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> </mfenced> </math> 

it is necessary to establish a bound on *R*. A bound on *R* then implies a bound on *x*[*i*] and *ω*[*t*+1,*i*] (if these variables are taken to be independent).

![equation](images/c9-disp-0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> </msub> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msub> <mo>max</mo> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="|" close="|"><msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mfenced> <mi>W</mi> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> </math> 

Thus,

![equation](images/c9-disp-0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>W</mi> <msup> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> </msub> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> 

It is interesting to note that unlike BEG, here there is no similar elimination of need for a bound on *ω*[*t* + 1,*i*] although there is the alternative:

![equation](images/c9-disp-0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub> <mi>W</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> </msub> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">ma</mi> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msqrt> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msqrt> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <munderover> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </msqrt> </math> 

For which

![equation](images/c9-disp-0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>W</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>X</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>.</mo> </math> 

Take ![images](images/c9-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>W</mi> <msubsup> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">Rb</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>then</mtext> </math>

![equation](images/c9-disp-0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">aL</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi mathvariant="italic">SA</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">bL</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mi>t</mi> </munder> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi mathvariant="italic">SA</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mi>a</mi> </mfrac> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>a</mi> </mfrac> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="italic">Rb</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>b</mi> </mfrac> <mo>+</mo> <mi>R</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi>c</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>c</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>W</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <msubsup> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </math> 

As with BEG, if ![images](images/c9-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>then with</mtext> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> </msub> <msqrt> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi mathvariant="italic">KW</mi> </mrow> </msqrt> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>W</mi> <msubsup> <mi>X</mi> <mo>&#8734;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> </math>

If ![images](images/c9-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>R</mi> </mfrac> <mtext>leads to</mtext> </math>

### 9.4.2 Loss Bounds Analysis Using Taylor Series for the sinh Link (SA) Algorithm

In order to consider the loss bounds for SA in the Taylor approximation approach it is necessary to solve for the distance function indicated by the link function (note: two notations have converged here where distance is denoted as d or Δ[*f*]:*d*(*s*,*ω*) = Δ[*f*](s, *ω*)):

![equation](images/c9-disp-0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup> <mi>d</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#969;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>&#969;</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi> </mfenced> <mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo> <mo>sin</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">h</mi> <mrow> <mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi> </mfenced> </math> 

Begin by taking the integral:
